name: Multivitamin
summary: A multivitamin combines several vitamins, often with minerals and sometimes other ingredients. Formulas differ, so the name alone does not tell you which nutrients or amounts a product contains.
commonUses: May fill gaps in a restricted diet
May lower the risk of heart disease or cancer
roles: Each vitamin or mineral has its own nutritional role; a combined product is not a separate nutrient.
Ingredients can overlap with individual supplements and fortified foods.

status.note: There is no single multivitamin status test. Tests for individual nutrients depend on the clinical question; this guide does not provide a routine status test.

high.note: See the cautions below; this guide does not establish a safe upper amount.

examples: A varied diet with vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, dairy or alternatives, and protein foods
foodSources.note: A multivitamin does not replace a varied diet.

forms.name: Vitamin and mineral combination
forms.note: The included nutrients and amounts vary by product; products with similar names are not necessarily equivalent.

forms.name: With or without iron
forms.note: Iron is not present in every formula. Its inclusion changes the safety considerations.

forms.name: Combination with other ingredients
forms.note: Some products also contain herbs or other supplements. Those ingredients need their own safety review.

reference.noUpperLimit: There is no upper limit for a multivitamin as a whole. Each vitamin and mineral in it has its own tolerable upper intake level, where one exists: see that nutrient's page and add up all products and fortified foods.

interactions.with: Warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists
interactions.note: Vitamin K in a multivitamin can change anticoagulation control. Discuss the exact formula and any changes with your anticoagulation clinician.
Excess preformed vitamin A, including retinol, can harm a developing baby. Discuss the formula and overlapping supplements with your clinician.

cautions: Overlapping products can add up to excessive intake. Check the full ingredient list alongside individual supplements and fortified foods.
Vitamin B6 can cause nerve damage with excessive ongoing exposure; it may appear in several products at once.
Excess preformed vitamin A, such as retinol, can damage the liver and is a particular concern during pregnancy.
Iron-containing products can cause nausea, abdominal pain and constipation. Their safety cannot be inferred from the word 'multivitamin'.

sources.title: Vitamin, Mineral, and Multivitamin Supplementation to Prevent Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement.
Multivitamin use and risk of cancer and cardiovascular disease in the Women's Health Initiative cohorts.

origin: A multivitamin is a manufactured product that combines several vitamins, often minerals and sometimes other ingredients, in one tablet, capsule or gummy.
There is no standard formula. Two products called multivitamins can differ in which nutrients they contain and in how much.
dosage: There is no single reference intake for a multivitamin, since each nutrient in it has its own value. Compare each ingredient on the label with that nutrient's own page.
Check the full label alongside other supplements and fortified foods, because amounts add up. Iron and vitamin A (retinol) are the ingredients to check first.

foodAmounts.verdict: Partly. A mixed diet supplies each vitamin and mineral from food, which is the whole point of a diet, but there is no single food amount that matches a multivitamin. This guide lists no figures; look at the individual nutrient pages for food amounts.

sources.title: Vitamin, Mineral, and Multivitamin Supplementation to Prevent Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement.
